323.title: Taking refuge formally
323.hook: many take the three refuges and five precepts before a monk or teacher
323.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists commonly repeat the three refuges and five precepts after a monk at temple gatherings; in Tibetan communities people take refuge from a lama and often receive a refuge name; in Zen a precepts ceremony (jukai) may include a dharma name and a small robe.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anjali, palms joined at the chest, and the handful of customs that make a temple guest welcome. Your line: shoes off.

In a temple hall, a young woman kneels in front of an older monk. Her family sits behind her. The monk says a line in Pali, and she repeats it. Then the next. Three lines, then the same three again, and a third time. Then five short promises. It takes about three minutes. Nothing flashes, nobody cries, and afterward there's tea. But she will remember this morning for the rest of her life.
screen: `A WOMAN KNEELS BEFORE A MONK.` → `THREE LINES, THREE TIMES.` → `FIVE SHORT PROMISES, THEN TEA.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in the Pali that Theravada Buddhists use: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge. I go to the teaching for refuge. I go to the community for refuge. Then again, with the word for second time, and again with the word for third time. Saying it three times marks it as meant. Then the five precepts, each worded as a training rule: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life, from taking what isn't given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicants that cloud the mind. You met each of them in the practices camp. Saraṇa means shelter, the place you run to in a storm. So refuge isn't joining a club or signing a creed. It's saying out loud where you turn when things get hard. Traditions do it differently. In the Theravada, people often repeat the refuges and precepts after a monk at many temple gatherings, again and again through life. In Tibetan communities there's a refuge ceremony with a lama, sometimes a tiny snip of hair, and a refuge name. In Zen, a ceremony of receiving the precepts may include a dharma name and a small sewn robe worn around the neck. And almost every teacher says the same thing: there's no rush. Some people take refuge in their first month. Some never do, and practice for decades. The door stays open. When you're ready.
screen: `THREE LINES, SAID THREE TIMES.` · `FIVE TRAINING RULES.` · `SARANA — A SHELTER IN A STORM.` · `THERAVADA, TIBETAN, ZEN.` · then, large: `WHEN YOU'RE READY.`

segments.voice: Sit beside one question without deciding anything: someday, would you want to take refuge formally? Yes, no and I don't know are all fine answers, so just notice what comes up, curiosity, hesitation, warmth or nothing at all, and don't argue with it. Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath.
Five precepts. The five training rules taken up, along with the three refuges, by anyone who formally takes refuge before a monk or teacher.
Your line: when you're ready. Where you already turn when things go wrong is a first answer to what refuge means for you. Day three hundred twenty-three, done.

324.title: The Buddhists you'll meet
324.hook: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, and many who simply sit: each a whole way
324.howItsDone: Buddhists practice through Theravada, Mahayana (including Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren) and Vajrayana traditions, and lay Buddhists often center their practice on giving, precepts, chanting and devotion rather than meditation; others meditate in non-sectarian insight or mindfulness groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five precepts, taken up with three lines said three times, and your line, when you're ready.

A potluck at a big-city Buddhist center, a little after noon. A Vietnamese grandmother quietly repeats the name of a Buddha under her breath. A Sri Lankan engineer mentions he'll be at the temple for the full moon. A young woman in a plain black robe has just come from a Zen sit. A Tibetan family arrives with a toddler and a thermos of butter tea. And a guy from the gym says he doesn't really call himself anything; he just sits every morning. They're all at the same table.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER REPEATING A NAME.` → `A FULL MOON, A BLACK ROBE, BUTTER TEA.` → `A GUY WHO JUST SITS.`

segments.voice: Buddhists often speak of vehicles, yana, and you've now met all three. The Theravada, the way of the elders, in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with the Pali canon, the alms round and the full-moon days. The Mahayana, the great vehicle, across China, Vietnam, Korea and Japan, with many schools inside it. Pure Land Buddhists recite the name of Amitabha Buddha, trusting in his vow; that's the grandmother at the potluck. Zen, called Chan in China and Seon in Korea, sits, and some of its lines work with the koans you met a few weeks back. Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra. The Vajrayana, the diamond vehicle, in Tibet, the Himalayas and Mongolia, with mantra, the teacher, and a day shaped by bodhicitta. And then many who simply sit, in insight meditation groups or with a meditation app; some call themselves Buddhist and some don't. Here's what surprises newcomers. In lay Buddhist life across Asia, meditation is often not the center of practice. Giving, keeping the precepts, chanting, bowing, caring for the monastery and the family dead: that's the practice, and it's a whole one. Each of these is a complete way, with its own texts, teachers and saints. They disagree on real things, and they've learned from one another for centuries. This path has tried to show each one on its own terms, and never to rank them. So when you meet a Buddhist, don't assume. Ask what their practice looks like; the answers vary more than you might expect. Many doors.
screen: `THERAVADA — THE WAY OF THE ELDERS.` · `MAHAYANA — PURE LAND, ZEN, NICHIREN.` · `VAJRAYANA — THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.` · `MANY WHO SIMPLY SIT.` · then, large: `MANY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Bring back the potluck table, the grandmother, the engineer, the woman in the black robe, the Tibetan family and the guy from the gym, and silently wish each one well: may your practice go well. Then wish the same to someone in your own life whose practice or faith differs from yours. Rest in the breath, which all of them share.
Yana. A vehicle: the word Buddhist traditions use for their own path, as in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana.
Your line: many doors. Each one opens on a whole way of its own. See you tomorrow.

325.title: Come and see
325.hook: many practice without taking refuge; the teaching invites you to come and see
325.carry: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours
325.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the Dhamma, including ehipassiko, in their devotions; teachers across traditions welcome people to practice without taking refuge or calling themselves Buddhist.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yana, the vehicles, and the Buddhists you might meet around one potluck table. Your line: many doors.

There's a certain kind of cook who, when you ask what's in the soup, doesn't explain. She just hands you a spoon. Don't take my word for it. Taste. It's a confident move: it only works if the soup is good. This week has been about practicing with people: a sangha, a friend, a temple, maybe taking refuge someday. But plenty of people practice for years without any of that, and the teaching doesn't check anyone's ID at the door. It hands you a spoon.
screen: `WHAT'S IN THE SOUP?` → `SHE HANDS YOU A SPOON.` → `TASTE IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: In Theravada temples and homes, people chant a short list of the qualities of the Buddha's teaching. In Pali it begins: "Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko, akāliko, ehipassiko." In plain English: the teaching is well spoken by the Blessed One, visible here and now, not a matter of time, and ehipassiko. Ehi means come. Passa means see. It's a word made from an invitation: the teaching is the come-and-see kind. Not come and believe. Not come and sign. The same list goes on to say it leads onward, and that the wise know it for themselves. You heard that spirit with the Kalamas, too: test it yourself. And in the old discourses, a listener often ends by saying something like: it's as if you set upright what was overturned, or held up a lamp in the dark so those with eyes could see. The lamp shows. The seeing is yours. That's one reason people can practice without any label. Some take refuge and some never do. Some come through a temple, some through a library book or an app like this one. The invitation doesn't change. So this stretch of the path, about practicing alongside other people, closes on an open door. Tomorrow the big lookout begins: six days to look back at the whole year, starting with the stories.
screen: `THE QUALITIES OF THE TEACHING.` · `EHI, COME. PASSA, SEE.` · `A LAMP HELD UP IN THE DARK.` · `NO LABEL NEEDED.` · then, large: `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, drop every label: you're not a Buddhist or a non-Buddhist, just someone breathing and seeing what's here. Watch one breath all the way in and all the way out, and ask whether watching brings a little more ease, or not. Don't decide in advance; come and see.
Ehipassiko. Come and see: the teaching invites you to look for yourself, not to believe first.
Your line: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours. No label required. That's day three hundred twenty-five.

Yes, you have to take refuge before any practice really counts.

326.title: Looking back: the stories
326.hook: the palace, the tree, the Deer Park, the sal trees
326.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's life at festivals such as Vesak, in temple murals and in children's classes, and many keep images of the four great scenes: the birth, the awakening, the first teaching and the passing away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ehipassiko, the teaching that says come and see, and your line, the lamp shows, the seeing is yours.
screen: `EHIPASSIKO — THE LAMP SHOWS, THE SEEING IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: At the end of a year, lots of people scroll back through their phone's photos. A birthday. A beach. A hospital waiting room. A dog. Things you'd forgotten, and things you never will. You're near the top of the first mountain now. For six days, the path turns around to look at what's behind you, one piece at a time. First, the stories: a whole life, from a palace to a grove of trees, that you've walked with since the start of the second camp.
screen: `SCROLLING BACK THROUGH THE YEAR.` → `NEAR THE TOP OF THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` → `FIRST, THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: The palace. A prince named Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, raised in three palaces, one for each season, with every comfort. Then four sights on the road with Channa: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a wanderer with a calm face. One night he looks in once at his sleeping wife Yasodhara and their newborn son, rides out on Kanthaka, and cuts off his hair by a river. The tree. Six years of starving himself, down to a handful of beans a day, until he remembers a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree as a boy. Sujata's bowl of rice. Eight handfuls of grass for a seat. I will not rise. Mara's army, and his hand reaching down to touch the earth. At dawn, awake. The Deer Park. Five old companions agree to ignore him, and then, as he comes near, they stand up. He teaches the middle way and the four truths, and Kondañña sees. The sal trees. Eighty years old, still walking, he eats his last meal from Cunda the smith and lies down between two sal trees that bloom out of season. His last words are about change and care; the last day of this year hears them in full. And around the four scenes, the people: Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed, the man with the finger garland who was told, I have stopped, you stop, and the Jataka animals, the hare in the moon and the golden goose. You don't need every detail. What stays is the shape: comfort, a question, a long search, a seat under a tree, a teaching given away, a good death. The stories stay.
screen: `THE PALACE — FOUR SIGHTS.` · `THE TREE — I WILL NOT RISE.` · `THE DEER PARK — THEY STOOD UP.` · `THE SAL TREES — THE LAST WORDS.` · then, large: `THE STORIES STAY.`

segments.voice: Pick whichever story from the year comes to mind first, and retell it to yourself silently, in a few sentences, as if to a child at bedtime. Don't check anything; whatever you remember is what stayed. Then let it settle, and sit with the breath, the way he sat under the tree.
Looking back. The palace, the tree, the Deer Park and the sal trees: the whole life, from comfort to a good death, as it stays with you.
Your line: the stories stay. They're yours to retell, in your own words. Until tomorrow.

327.title: Looking back: the practices
327.hook: metta, breath, walking, precepts, giving, the holy days
327.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists typically build a few practices into ordinary life: metta and breath meditation, walking meditation, keeping the five precepts, giving to monasteries and others, and keeping the moon days and festivals of their tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stories, from the palace to the sal trees, and your line, the stories stay.

A new driver grips the wheel with both hands and says each step under her breath: mirror, signal, look. Every turn is a small exam. A year later she merges onto the highway while talking about dinner. She doesn't remember the lessons. Her hands just know. Something like that can happen with a year of practice. The practices came one at a time, often a little clumsily. Somewhere along the way, some of them may have stopped being lessons and started being things you do.
screen: `MIRROR, SIGNAL, LOOK.` → `A YEAR LATER, TALKING ABOUT DINNER.` → `LESSONS BECOME WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: Metta. Four phrases wishing safety and ease, first to yourself, then to a benefactor, a dear friend, a neutral person, a difficult one, and finally to all beings, as the metta sutta puts it, like a mother protecting her only child. The breath. Sixteen steps of breathing mindfully: knowing the long breath and the short one, the whole body, joy and ease, the mind, and change. Counting when the mind is busy. Naming the hindrances when they arrive. Walking. A short lane, lifting, moving, placing, and the turn at the end, where you notice the wanting to turn before you turn. Walking in the city, too. The precepts. The three refuges and the five training rules: not killing, not taking, care in sex, true speech, a clear mind. And when you break one: notice, make amends, begin again. Giving. Giving first, before you feel ready. The giver who is glad three times: before, while, and after. The poor woman's lamp that burned longest. Giving attention, and giving without a receipt. The holy days. The full and new moons of the uposatha, Vesak and the baby Buddha's bath, lanterns on the water, the rains retreat, and Kathina, when the robes are given. That's a lot, and nobody keeps all of it every day. The point was never to collect practices. It was to find the few that fit your life, and let them become what your hands already know. You practice now.
screen: `METTA — FROM YOURSELF TO ALL BEINGS.` · `THE BREATH AND THE LANE.` · `THE PRECEPTS AND GIVING.` · `THE HOLY DAYS.` · then, large: `YOU PRACTICE NOW.`

segments.voice: Take a quick tour: one silent metta phrase for yourself, may I be at ease; three slow steps, lifting, moving, placing; one small precept held in mind for the next hour; and one thing you could give today. Then sit, and let the breath be the whole practice, long or short, just as it is. Another day, each of these can have a full minute of its own.
Looking back. Metta, the breath, walking, the precepts, giving and the holy days: the practices of the year, now yours to keep.
Your line: you practice now. The few that fit your life are enough. Day three hundred twenty-seven, done.

328.title: Looking back: the Dhammapada
328.howItsDone: Buddhists across the Theravada world memorize and recite verses of the Dhammapada, hear them in sermons, and teach them to children; many keep a copy for a lifetime and return to favorite verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the practices, from metta to the holy days, and your line, you practice now.

Most people have started a big book and never finished it. It sits on the nightstand with a bookmark stuck at page forty, quietly judging. This year you did something a lot of people never do: you read a whole book of scripture, cover to cover, a few verses at a time, over seventy-five days. At the end, you picked ten verses that stayed with you and wrote them down. Somewhere, maybe on a scrap of paper or in your phone, those ten are waiting.
screen: `A BOOKMARK STUCK AT PAGE FORTY.` → `THIS YEAR, A WHOLE BOOK.` → `TEN VERSES, WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada: the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching. Four hundred twenty-three verses in twenty-six chapters, the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings across the Theravada world, carried across Asia in several languages, and brought into English by Max Müller in the nineteenth century. You began with the twin verses. In Müller's translation, the very first line is: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." A few verses later came the one many people remember first: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Then the chapters rolled on. Earnestness. Thought, and the body fragile as a jar. Flowers. The fool and the wise. The thousands, where conquering yourself beats conquering a thousand thousand men. Evil and good, filling the water-pot drop by drop. Old age. Self. The Buddha, whose teaching fits in one line: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Happiness, where contentment is the greatest wealth. Anger. Other people's faults, so easy to see. The way. The elephant. Thirst, and the best gift, the gift of the teaching. And at the end, the mendicant and the brahmana, the one who is truly worthy. A verse you read months ago may mean something different now. Not because the verse changed. You did. That's why people keep this book for a lifetime: not to finish it, but to come back. Twenty-six chapters, read whole. The verses stay.

329.title: Looking back: the depths
329.hook: the immeasurables, mindfulness, emptiness, koans, the elders, the diamond vehicle
329.tomorrow: The first mountain, from the top
329.howItsDone: Buddhists often spend years or a lifetime with one of these depths: the brahmaviharas, satipatthana practice, the Heart Sutra, koan study, or the Theravada and Tibetan paths, usually with a teacher and a community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Dhammapada, twenty-six chapters read whole, and your line, the verses stay.

From a boat, the sea is a flat blue surface. Put on a mask and lower your face into the water, and there's a whole world down there: a reef, colors, a turtle drifting past as if it had all day. The flat blue was never the whole story. The fifth camp was that moment. The stories, the practices and the book were the surface; the depths put your face in the water.
screen: `FROM THE BOAT, FLAT BLUE.` → `FACE IN THE WATER.` → `A WHOLE WORLD DOWN THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the four immeasurables, four rooms to live in: metta, karuna, mudita and upekkha. Loving-kindness, compassion, gladness at others' joy, and equanimity, each, as later teachers put it, with a near enemy that looks like it: pity for compassion, indifference for equanimity. Then the Satipatthana, the direct path: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience, watched ardently, aware and mindful. The second arrow you don't have to shoot. Knowing without fixing. Seven years, or seven days. Then the Heart Sutra. Form is emptiness, and emptiness is not nothing. No eye, no ear. Nothing to attain, and so, without fear. Gate, gate. Then the koans, which you weren't supposed to solve. Mu. Wash your bowl. The flag and the wind. Every day is a good day. The sound of one hand. Then two electives, side by side, never ranked. The way of the elders: three baskets, forest monks, rules as a shelter, calm and insight, rising and falling, entering the stream, Buddhaghosa's path of virtue, calm and wisdom. And the diamond vehicle: the six syllables, wheels and flags, the four thoughts, the teacher, tonglen, the slogans, bodhicitta, Tara, the sand swept into the river, the bardo. Each of these could fill a lifetime, and for some people it does. You've had a first look. The Buddha said the teaching he found was deep and hard to see; a year in, that line holds a little more. And this week's lines: when you're ready, many doors, come and see, the stories stay, you practice now, the verses stay. Today: there's more.
screen: `FOUR ROOMS TO LIVE IN.` · `THE DIRECT PATH.` · `EMPTINESS AND THE KOANS.` · `THE ELDERS AND THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.` · then, large: `THERE'S MORE.`

segments.voice: If you have the time, sit longer today, up to twenty minutes: when the two-minute sit ends, simply keep going, and if you can't, two minutes is a whole sit. Choose nothing special, no technique and no room from the depths in particular. Just sit, and let whatever the year has planted do its quiet work.
Looking back. The immeasurables, mindfulness, emptiness, koans, the elders and the diamond vehicle: a first look at depths that go much further.
Your line: there's more. Any one of those rooms is there to come back to. That closes the week.
